nodes.label: David Arnold
nodes.description: A historian of South Asia, and a founding member of the Subaltern Studies collective, whose work brings medicine, science and environment into the study of colonial power. Colonizing the Body (1993) studies state medicine and epidemic disease in nineteenth-century India. The introduction to Science, Technology and Medicine in Colonial India (2000) rejects a single trajectory from European discovery to passive reception overseas. Drawing on Steven Shapin’s account of knowledge as socially situated, it insists that a history of science in India must also be a history of India. It criticizes George Basalla’s diffusion model for flattening differences among colonial situations, marginalizing local agency and assuming a beneficial sequence of development, while also rejecting accounts that understate colonial disruption. His environmental histories include The Problem of Nature (1996) and The Tropics and the Traveling Gaze (2006).

nodes.label: J. R. McNeill
nodes.description: An environmental historian who works at global and regional scales. Something New Under the Sun (2000) is an environmental history of the twentieth-century world. Mosquito Empires (2010) argues that ecological change made the Greater Caribbean hospitable to the mosquitoes that carry yellow fever and malaria. Because survivors gained immunity or resistance, these diseases took sides in the struggles for empire and revolution between 1620 and 1914, decimating forces sent from Europe. His survey of the field credits the Annales with an inspiring general approach while noting how little environmental history its founders wrote, and treats Alfred Crosby’s studies of ecological exchange as landmarks. In his 2020 AHA presidential address he argues that scientific evidence can illuminate histories poorly documented in writing, while warning against monocausal climate histories and against letting a new tool dictate the question.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: Something New Under the Sun (2000); “Observations on the Nature and Culture of Environmental History” (2003); Mosquito Empires: Ecology and War in the Greater Caribbean, 1620–1914 (2010).

nodes.label: Sheila Fitzpatrick
nodes.description: A historian of the Soviet Union and of Stalinism from below. In ‘Revisionism in Retrospect’ (2008) she gives a participant’s account of how social historians of the 1970s and 1980s challenged political scientists’ totalitarian model, crediting revisionism with an appreciation of contingency and a new approach to power and to the interplay of government and society. Stalin’s Peasants: Resistance and Survival in the Russian Village after Collectivization (1994) and Everyday Stalinism: Ordinary Life in Extraordinary Times (1999) carry that social history into village and city. In a comparative chapter with Alf Lüdtke on Nazism and Stalinism, she treats Hannah Arendt’s thesis of social atomization as a question for research: social bonds were broken but also remade, and participation involved people’s emotional investments.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: The Russian Revolution (1982; revisions 1994, 2007 and 2017 distinct); Stalin’s Peasants (1994); Everyday Stalinism (1999).

nodes.label: Patrick J. Geary
nodes.description: A medieval historian of relics, memory and ethnic identity. Furta Sacra (1978) studied thefts of relics in the central Middle Ages, and his essay ‘Sacred Commodities’ (1986) asks what made relics exchangeable within a particular medieval setting rather than assuming a timeless market. Phantoms of Remembrance (1994) concerns memory and oblivion at the end of the first millennium. The Myth of Nations (2002) uses research on changing early medieval identities to criticize modern nationalist claims to ancient continuity; Steven Fanning credits its central argument while warning that its survey contains questionable assertions and broad generalizations.

nodes.label: Mike Davis
nodes.description: A historian of cities, capitalism and environmental disaster. City of Quartz (1990) and Ecology of Fear (1998) examined the political economy and ecology of Los Angeles. Late Victorian Holocausts (2001) argues that the famines of the late nineteenth century arose from the interaction of El Niño droughts with imperial and market systems that left populations vulnerable, not from weather alone; it opens from Raymond Williams’s reflection on nature and human history. Davis recalls that Robert Brenner’s UCLA seminar on Capital, which moved on to crisis theory and twentieth-century economic history, gave him the confidence to pursue his own agenda. He later criticized Marx and Engels for saying nothing about cities and for leaving the patriarchy of the workers’ movement unchallenged.

nodes.label: Hugh Trevor-Roper
nodes.description: A historian of early modern Britain and Europe. His 1959 essay on ‘The General Crisis of the Seventeenth Century’, prompted, as Blair Worden notes, by Eric Hobsbawm’s Marxist analysis of the century’s revolts, set the English revolution within a wider European crisis; the later preface to his essays questions a simple Calvinism-to-capitalism explanation associated with Weber and Tawney. Worden explains his resistance to deterministic accounts of revolution, including Christopher Hill’s, and his attention to contingency and personality. In his chapter for Hobsbawm and Terence Ranger’s The Invention of Tradition (1983) he argued that the kilt, clan tartans and the very idea of a distinct Highland culture, to which Scots ascribe great antiquity, are largely modern, developed after the Union with England; The Invention of Scotland (2008) extends the theme. His authentication of the forged Hitler diaries in 1983 was a serious failure of judgment.

nodes.label: Peter Gay
nodes.description: A historian of European intellectual and cultural life who joined social history to psychoanalysis. The Enlightenment: An Interpretation (1966, 1969), Weimar Culture (1968) and the five-volume The Bourgeois Experience: Victoria to Freud (1984–98) are his major studies, and Freud: A Life for Our Time (1988) is his biography of Freud. In a 1997 interview he describes Freud as an indispensable resource for studying the interplay of psychological processes and external circumstances, insisting that an event such as the French Revolution still requires attention to state finances, royal prestige and social conflict. He criticized psychohistory that gave inner experience too much causal weight.

nodes.label: Paul Thompson
nodes.description: A social and oral historian concerned with how interviews change both historical evidence and research practice. His retrospective interview credits Townsend’s socially engaged research and George Ewart Evans’s listening methods, and recalls resisting Hobsbawm’s request to remove oral-history material from The Edwardians. Thompson distinguishes his early emphasis on reliable recollection from later attention to subjectivity, silence and memory associated with Passerini and Portelli. His community-history discussion also warns that participation can exclude less confident people and need not produce progressive politics. Becky Taylor’s reassessment credits the fishing project’s attention to change and its preservation of sources, while questioning interview schedules, uneven transcription and the insufficiently examined category of fisherman. Her reuse demonstrates how an archive can support questions its makers did not fully pursue. Living the Fishing was collaborative work with Tony Wailey and Trevor Lummis, not Thompson’s solitary project.

nodes.label: Kathleen Wilson
nodes.description: A historian of Britain and its eighteenth-century empire. In her introduction to A New Imperial History, Wilson argues that imperial encounters helped constitute identities within Britain as well as overseas. Difference is an instrument of power, while identities are historically imposed and negotiated through legal status, gender, slavery and performance. She uses Chakrabarty’s challenge to Europe as history’s universal subject and Catherine Hall’s insistence on theorizing difference, without proposing that cultural analysis replace political or social history. Her account of colonial governmentality draws explicitly on Foucault. The later Strolling Players of Empire continues the inquiry through performance and colonial rule. Her work therefore connects cultural and political explanation; it does not treat every imperial setting as identical or empire as a one-way export from a metropolitan centre.

nodes.label: Charles E. Rosenberg
nodes.description: A historian of medicine and science. The Cholera Years (1962), on the United States in 1832, 1849 and 1866, is credited with leading historians to study not only a disease and its victims but society’s response to it, through politics, law and social mores. The Care of Strangers (1987), a history of the American hospital, and Explaining Epidemics (1992) continued that social history of medicine. In a 2013 interview he places his work within a social-medicine tradition that treats medical ideas and access to care as embedded in society, questions tidy genealogies in which translated theorists alone changed historical research, and distinguishes psychiatric diagnostic categories that organize research and care from explanations of mechanism.

nodes.label: Robert Bartlett
nodes.description: A medieval historian of conquest, law and historical categories. Trial by Fire and Water (1986) studied the medieval judicial ordeal, and The Making of Europe (1993) traced conquest, colonization and cultural change between 950 and 1350. His 2001 article on race and ethnicity treats both terms as social constructions and warns against using present administrative labels as ready-made historical explanations. Comparing medieval terminology, he emphasizes culture, law, language and religion in the making of identities, while examining genealogical idioms of descent, and separates collective identity from any automatic demand for sovereign statehood. Geraldine Heng later questions the sharpness of his distinction between medieval cultural difference and biological racism.

nodes.label: Stephen Greenblatt
nodes.description: A literary scholar and theorist whose New Historicism reads literature within the whole field of a period’s culture. Renaissance Self-Fashioning (1980) examines how More, Tyndale, Wyatt, Spenser, Marlowe and Shakespeare fashioned selves, finding that new questions about identity shaped sixteenth-century writing. He calls New Historicism ‘madly eclectic’: it grew from impatience with American formalism and with Marxist criticism, and drew on Foucault to escape the base/superstructure dichotomy, as well as on Walter Benjamin, Michel de Certeau and Clifford Geertz. He credits Raymond Williams with showing how to connect art to the world in which it is made. Sarah Maza questions how far New Historicism and historians’ cultural history actually meet across disciplinary lines, and John Monfasani criticized The Swerve for opposing medieval darkness to Renaissance modernity; Greenblatt replied defending the Renaissance and the importance of atomism.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: Renaissance Self-Fashioning (1980); Shakespearean Negotiations (1988); Marvelous Possessions (1991).
